title: Quantifying and Optimizing Simplicity via Polynomial Representations
claim: Sample interpolation paths through a model's function landscape and fit polynomials to them. The effective degree of the fit measures simplicity.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right with big arrow, 3D landscape then 2x2 path/histogram grid
description: Left panel, titled 'Neural Function', shows a 3D translucent surface for f(x) over Dimension i and Dimension j. Small real image thumbnails (trucks, horse, bird, frog) mark data points. Colored dotted paths (blue, green, red, purple) connect data points, with endpoints x1 and x2 and an interpolation parameter alpha labeled. A legend separates real data from interpolated points. A large gray arrow leads to the right panel, 'Polynomial Representation'. That panel is a 2x2 grid, one cell per path (Path1 to Path4). Each cell has a color-matched curve of output versus interpolation alpha, plus a bar histogram of coefficients c0 to c5 with an ED value (3.00, 8.13, 4.11, 3.22). The effective-degree formula, ED(f) = E_path[Σ|c_k|·k] = 4.62, sits at the bottom. The eye goes first to the colorful 3D landscape, then to the path grid.
caption: Method overview. Left: An illustration of the functional landscape of a neural function f by sampling interpolation paths between data points. Right: The function f’s output along these paths is approximated using polynomial expansions. Coefficient histograms reveal the complexity: smoother paths (e.g., Path1) yield low-degree coefficients, whereas oscillating paths (e.g., Path2) show significant high-degree components. The effective degree (ED), computed by averaging coefficient-weighted degrees of fitted polynomials over multiple interpolation paths, serves as a differentiable proxy for functional simplicity.
abstract: Deep networks often exhibit a preference for "simple" solutions, and such a simplicity bias is widely believed to play a key role in generalization. Yet a broadly applicable, quantitative measure of simplicity remains elusive. We introduce polynomial representations as a distribution-aware, low-dimensional surrogate for neural functions: we approximate a network's predictive behavior along data-dependent interpolation paths using orthogonal polynomial bases, yielding a compact functional representation. We show that the effective degree of this representation serves as a practical simplicity metric that is predictive of generalization across tasks and architectures, and consistently outperforms existing generalization proxies such as sharpness. Finally, polynomial representations naturally yield a differentiable simplicity regularizer, which consistently improves generalization in image and text classification, fine-tuning contrastive vision-language models, and reinforcement learning.
